Doings
doo'ingz
n. pl. (deeds, practices, the whole course of a man's or a people's conduct; rendering Hebrew maalal and alilah)
From do, Saxon don. Hebrew maalal is from alal, to act or work upon, and denotes practices rather than single acts — which is why the prophets so often pair it with ways: a man's doings are his habits made visible.

Biblical Definition

Doings is the prophets' word for a settled course of conduct, and it is nearly always used where God is weighing a people rather than an individual act. Hosea states the principle of exact recompense: “I will punish them for their ways, and reward them their doings” (Hosea 4:9) — and the clause before it, like people, like priest, refuses the clergy any exemption. Jeremiah names them as the reason judgment is coming on the house of David: God's fury will burn “because of the evil of your doings” (Jeremiah 21:12), in a verse whose first half commands the king to execute judgment in the morning and deliver the spoiled out of the oppressor's hand. What God indicts is not merely private vice but a court that would not do justice. Micah puts the sharp question to a people who resented such preaching: “is the spirit of the LORD straitened? are these his doings?” (Micah 2:7) — that is, is the fault in God or in you? Ezekiel shows what grace produces when it comes: “Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that were not good, and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight” (Ezekiel 36:31), and the order is decisive. The self-loathing comes after the promised new heart, not before it. And the word serves for God's own acts too: “declare among the people his doings” (Psalm 9:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Deeds and settled practices. The prophets weigh a people by their doings, God rewards them exactly, and Ezekiel shows true shame for them arriving after the new heart, not before it.

expand to see more

DOINGS, n. plu. Things done; transactions; feats; actions, good or bad.

2. Conduct; behavior; course of life.

3. Stir; bustle; as, here is fine doings.

4. In Scripture, the practices of a people considered as a whole; as, the evil of your doings, Jer. 21.

5. Also of God's acts; declare among the people his doings, Ps. 9.

Key Scripture

Hosea 4:9 — "And there shall be, like people, like priest: and I will punish them for their ways, and reward them their doings."

Jeremiah 21:12 — "O house of David, thus saith the LORD; Execute judgment in the morning, and deliver him that is spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor, lest my fury go out like fire, and burn that none can quench it, because of the evil of your doings."

Ezekiel 36:31 — "Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that were not good, and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations."

Psalm 9:11 — "Sing praises to the LORD, which dwelleth in Zion: declare among the people his doings."

Modern Corruption

Conduct is separated from worship, so that a people's doings are treated as a private matter beside their profession — the exact division Hosea and Jeremiah were sent to destroy.

expand to see more

The prophets confront a religion in good working order. The feasts were kept, the priesthood functioned, the temple stood — and God pronounced against the nation because of its doings: false weights, a court that would not deliver the oppressed, and priests no better than the people they served. Hosea's like people, like priest forecloses the modern instinct that leadership failure is a separate category from congregational compromise; the two rise and fall together. Wherever a church becomes exact about doctrine and vague about practice, or exact about practice and vague about doctrine, the prophets have something to say, and Micah's question waits at the end of it: are these his doings? The fault is never in God.

The principle to recover is Ezekiel's order. God says he will sprinkle clean water, give a new heart, take away the stony heart, put his Spirit within — and then shall ye remember your own evil ways and lothe yourselves (Ezekiel 36:25-31). Repentance of this depth is a fruit of regeneration, not a qualification for it. This is the monergistic pattern the whole Reformed doctrine of conversion rests on: the new heart is given, and the loathing of the old doings follows. A man who waits until he is sufficiently ashamed before he comes to Christ has the order backwards and will wait for ever.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maalal is a deed or practice, usually in the plural and usually under judgment; alilah is an act or exploit, used of God's doings as well as man's.

expand to see more

Hebrew maalal (H4611) — doings, practices; the prophets' standard term for a settled course of conduct.

Hebrew alilah (H5949) — an act, a deed, an exploit; used of the LORD's doings in Psalm 9:11.

Hebrew derek (H1870) — way; regularly paired with doings, the road and the walking of it.

Greek praxis (G4234) — a doing, a practice; put off the deeds of the old man, Colossians 3:9.

Greek ergon (G2041) — work, deed; that which a man has actually done.

Usage

"Of exact recompense on priest and people alike: I will punish them for their ways, and reward them their doings (Hosea 4:9)."

"Of judgment on an unjust court: because of the evil of your doings (Jeremiah 21:12)."

"Of shame following the new heart: shall lothe yourselves in your own sight (Ezekiel 36:31)."
